::: {#thm-double-plus-power-closed}
#### A closed form for $b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n$

Let $b_0, b_1, \ldots$ be the sequence with $b_0 = 0$ and $b_n = 2 b_{n-1} + 2^n$ for every integer $n \ge 1$
(@exm-double-plus-power-sequence).
Then $b_n = n \cdot 2^n$ for every non-negative integer (@def-nonnegative-integers) $n$.

:::

::: {.content-hidden when-format="revealjs"}

{{< slidebreak >}}

::: proof

We use induction (@def-proof-by-induction), following @rem-induction-template with $n_0 = 0$.
Let $P(n)$ be the equation $b_n = n \cdot 2^n$.

**Base case.**
$b_0 = 0 = 0 \cdot 2^0$.

**Inductive step.**
Let $k \ge 0$ be an integer, and suppose $P(k)$: $b_k = k \cdot 2^k$.
The goal $P(k + 1)$ is $b_{k + 1} = (k + 1) \cdot 2^{k + 1}$.
Since $k + 1 \ge 1$, the recurrence relation gives $b_{k + 1}$, and

$$
\ba
b_{k + 1}
&= 2 b_k + 2^{k + 1}
&& \text{(recurrence relation)}
\\&= 2 \cdot k \cdot 2^k + 2^{k + 1}
&& \text{(induction hypothesis)}
\\&= k \cdot 2^{k + 1} + 2^{k + 1}
\\&= (k + 1) \cdot 2^{k + 1}.
\ea
$$

So $P(k + 1)$ holds, and by induction $b_n = n \cdot 2^n$ for every non-negative integer $n$.

:::

:::
